a: New Orleans, the city where he grew up
Monticello, Thomas Jefferson's former home
The Whitney Plantation in Louisiana

questions.q: What point does Smith make about Confederate statues and street names?
a: They keep slavery's history visible in public life
They are harmless reminders of the distant past
They have all been removed from the city
They honor soldiers who opposed slavery
questions.why: Lesson one says the statues, parks and buildings keep the history of enslaved people embedded in everyday places.

questions.q: What realization does Smith reach after visiting the plantations and Angola prison?
a: America's wealth was built on the labor of enslaved Black people
The South's economy grew without slave labor
Plantation owners treated their workers fairly
Most enslaved people were paid for their work
questions.why: Lesson two says that wherever he went, the country's developed and luxurious communities came from Black labor.

questions.q: What does the summary say about Black wealth in America today?
a: Black Americans own less than four percent of the country's wealth
Black Americans now own just over ten percent of the wealth
Black Americans own roughly half of the country's wealth
Black Americans own about a quarter of the country's wealth
questions.why: Lesson three notes that two centuries after slavery, Black communities own under four percent of the nation's wealth.

questions.q: Why does the summary describe freed Black people as starting at a late starting line?
a: They lacked education, money and social standing after slavery
